title: Gap Launches "Denim On Your Own," a Fall 2026 Campaign Starring Malcolm Todd and Inde Navarrette
body_text: Gap Launches "Denim On Your Own," a Fall 2026 Campaign Starring Malcolm Todd and Inde Navarrette by Gap Gap August 11, 2026 Continuing its legacy of championing emerging artists, Gap brings music and style together to celebrate Gap Denim and individuality This Fall, Gap unveils "Denim on your own," its Fall 2026 campaign starring musician Malcolm Todd and actress Inde Navarrette. Set to Malcolm Todd's original rendition of Robyn's iconic anthem "Dancing on My Own," created specifically for this campaign, Gap brings together two rising talents from different creative worlds. United by a shared confidence but distinct in their perspectives, the campaign showcases Malcolm and Inde alongside GapDenim as a canvas for their creativity and personal style. With this campaign, Gap continues to serve as a platform for the next generation of creative voices, championing emerging artists who are shaping culture through music, art, and self-expression. Through this creative collaboration with Malcolm Todd and Inde Navarrette, Gap reinforces its commitment to fostering authentic partnerships that spotlight new talent and celebrate individuality. “Gap has always been at the intersection of music, style, and culture — partnering with artists who bring a unique point of view and inspire people to express themselves,” said Mark Breitbard, President and CEO of Gap brand. “From our heritage of iconic creative collaborations to championing today’s emerging voices, we continue to evolve how we show up in culture — building our own cultural currency through authentic partnerships, original storytelling, and a clear point of view.” The campaign is directed by Tanu Muiño with creative direction from Calvin Leung, Head of Gap Brand Creative, fashion and image by Alastair McKimm, and photography by Bjorn Loos. The campaign follows Malcolm and Inde through a series of distinct spaces, where each expresses their own rhythm and style. Grounded in a shared belief that personal style is a powerful form of expression, "Denim on your own" reflects how Gap's timeless essentials become part of the everyday lives of artists as they create, perform, and connect with their audiences. “For this campaign, we didn’t simply ask Malcolm to cover ‘Dancing On My Own,’ we asked him to reinterpret the song through his own perspective,” said Fabiola Torres, Chief Marketing Officer of Gap brand. “That same spirit of making something your own defines GapDenim — a collection designed for people to find the fits and styles that feel uniquely theirs. It’s how Gap has connected with culture for generations, and how we continue to inspire originality today.” Malcolm Todd is one of music's most exciting emerging artists. He’s known for his catchy and playful approach to songwriting and production. With multiple songs having reached platinum status and his latest album, Do That Again, out via Columbia Records having debuted in the top 5 of the billboard charts Malcolm is now preparing for his instantly sold out of his 38 date North American tour launching September 2. Inde Navarrette is one of Hollywood's most exciting rising talents, fresh off the breakout success of OBSESSION, the critically acclaimed global box office phenomenon, and recognized for bringing authenticity and emotional depth to every role. Though they come from different creative worlds, both Malcolm and Inde share the same spirit: a commitment to doing things their own way. “I’ve always been drawn to making things my own — whether that’s through music, style, or the way I express myself,” said Malcolm Todd. “Being able to reinterpret an iconic song like ‘Dancing on My Own’ and bring my own perspective to it was such a special experience. I like to trust my instincts and not overthink things. To be part of a Gap campaign on such a big set, surrounded by so much creativity, and still feel like I could just be myself was really meaningful.” "From the moment we started filming the Gap campaign, it felt like we were able to bring our own energy and personalities to the campaign," said Inde Navarrette. "There was so much freedom to move, experiment and express ourselves. That’s what makes style so personal — it’s about feeling confident in who you are and showing up as yourself.” Since 1969, Gap Denim has been a defining part of the brand’s identity, creating styles that have become part of everyday wardrobes around the world. The Fall 2026 collection builds on that legacy with a focus on fit, versatility and personal style, featuring refreshed washes, utility-inspired colorways, updated silhouettes and modern takes on Gap’s iconic denim codes. Anchored by new style expressions like the Mid-Rise Straight Taper Jean, seen on Inde, alongside classic favorites like the ‘90s Loose Jean, worn by Malcolm, GapDenim gives individuals the freedom to discover the fits and styles that feel uniquely their own. The Fall 2026 "Denim on your own" campaign launches today across Gap's digital and social channels, email, stores, out-of-home with billboards in NYC Times Square and Sunset Boulevard, gap.com, paid media running across YouTube, TikTok, Meta, Pinterest, and creator partnerships. Follow along at @gap, @malcolmtodd and @indenavarrette. About Gap: Gap is a globally recognized icon of casual American style. Founded in San Francisco in 1969, Gap champions originality by creating loved essentials and delivering culturally relevant experiences that celebrate individuality. Gap is a lifestyle brand offering products across generations, including GapKids, babyGap, Gap Maternity, GapBody, GapFit, Gap Accessories and Gap Beauty, as well as GapStudio and partner collaborations through GapX. Gap is the namesake brand of the global specialty retailer, Gap Inc. (NYSE: GAP) and connects with customers online and in company-operated and franchise retail locations globally. For more information, visit gap.com . Press Contact: Gap | PR Consulting gap@prconsulting.net jenna_stone@gap.com Don’t miss out on the latest Gap Inc. news! Sign-up to get email alerts about news on Gap Inc. and our brands. Categories Press Release

title: What Privacy Cards Are and Why They Belong in Your Wallet
summary: Privacy cards protect your real card number from merchants and data breaches. Learn how they work and why they belong in your wallet.
body_text: Every time you type your card number into a checkout form, you hand that number to a merchant and trust them to protect it forever. That trust is often misplaced. Over 421 million credit and debit card records were exposed in U.S. data breaches in 2024 alone, and the problem accelerated in 2025. If your card number gets stolen even once, the ripple effects can take months to untangle. Privacy cards exist to break that chain entirely by giving merchants a number that is not connected to your real account in any meaningful way. This guide explains what privacy cards are, how they work, when to use them, and how they fit into a broader strategy for protecting both your financial security and your household budget. Key Takeaways Privacy cards shield your real card number: A privacy card is a digital payment card with a virtual card number, expiration date, and CVV, just like a normal card, but the merchant sees only that privacy card number, not your underlying account details. If that number leaks, your actual bank account is untouched. Fraud is rising fast and your primary card is the target: E-commerce fraud is expected to rise from $44.3 billion in 2024 to $107 billion by 2029, a growth of 141%. Every year you delay using privacy cards, the threat landscape grows larger. Start using one for unfamiliar merchants now. Subscription control is one of the biggest practical benefits: A Forbes survey found that around 47% of people pay for subscription services they don't use. A dedicated privacy card per subscription lets you cut off billing with a single tap rather than navigating cancellation flows. Spending limits turn privacy cards into budgeting tools: You can set customizable spending limits on cards to track and maintain budgets at specific merchants and block hidden fees. If your actual spending is already near the limit, treat that as a signal to review the category. Limitations exist and are worth knowing upfront: Privacy cards work best for online purchases. They may not work for in-store pickups that require presenting a physical card, car rentals, or hotel check-ins that need the original card. Always carry a backup payment method. Quick-Start Prioritization Framework Strategy Best For Effort Level Time to Results Single-use card for one-off purchases Anyone buying from an unfamiliar site Low Immediate Merchant-locked card per subscription People with 3+ recurring bills Low Immediate Spending-limit card per budget category Households tracking monthly spending Medium 1-2 billing cycles Category-locked card (groceries, dining) Budgeters who want automated guardrails Medium 1-2 weeks Full virtual card system + budgeting app Anyone wanting complete financial visibility High 1 month Start here if you're: New to privacy cards: Set up one single-use card for your next online purchase from a store you haven't used before. The setup takes under five minutes and the protection is immediate. Drowning in subscriptions: Create one merchant-locked privacy card per recurring service. If a service tries to raise its price without warning, the card's spending limit blocks the overcharge automatically. Focused on household budgeting: Pair virtual cards with a structured budgeting tool. Envelope connects virtual debit cards directly to digital spending envelopes, so the card can only draw from the money you've already allocated for that category. How Privacy Cards Actually Work The Basic Mechanics Every virtual card is connected to your bank account but comes with a unique 16-digit card number, CVV, and expiration date. The provider directly debits your funding source for transactions as you make them. From the merchant's perspective, it looks like a completely normal card transaction. From your perspective, you've handed over a number that is disposable. When you use a virtual card number for a purchase, the merchant never sees your actual card details. If that merchant gets breached, the attackers only get a virtual number, your real card remains untouched. This is a fundamental shift from how traditional card payments work. With a regular debit or credit card, a breach at any one of the dozens of merchants you've paid over the years can expose an account you rely on every day. Card Types and What Each One Does Most privacy card providers offer several card configurations. Understanding the differences helps you choose the right tool for each situation. Single-use cards self-destruct after one completed transaction. Once the payment settles, the card number becomes permanently invalid, any future charge attempt against that number gets declined. These are best for one-time purchases from unfamiliar websites. Merchant-locked cards bind themselves to whichever merchant processes the first transaction. After that, the card only works at that one merchant. If a different merchant tries to charge the card, the transaction fails. This makes merchant-locked cards a natural fit for subscriptions because they keep working at the same store but are useless if the card data leaks elsewhere. Category-locked cards control your spending and are declined at merchants that do not fit into specific categories. This type is particularly useful for households that want to apply automatic guardrails to categories like dining, entertainment, or groceries. Pro Tip: For free trials, use a single-use card set to the exact trial cost. The card closes after the first charge, which means the merchant physically cannot bill you when the trial ends, regardless of whether you remember to cancel. The Fraud Landscape That Makes Privacy Cards Necessary Why Your Primary Card is Constantly at Risk In the first quarter of 2025 alone, there were 154,483 credit card fraud reports filed, a 24% increase from the previous quarter. That surge reflects a structural problem: every transaction you make with your primary card leaves that number with another merchant, another database, another potential breach target. The scale of recent breaches makes this concrete. 560 million people had their payment and personal information exposed when Ticketmaster fell victim to a cyberattack in May 2024. That single breach affected more people than the entire population of the United States. Therefore, rather than assuming any merchant is breach-proof, the practical move is to give each merchant a number that is worthless if stolen. Phishing contributes to 40% of all online fraud losses, and it remains the most common and successful attack vector. Privacy cards don't stop phishing attempts, but they limit the damage. Even if a phisher captures a virtual card number, that number can be locked, paused, or closed before significant harm occurs. The Cost of Doing Nothing The total cost impact on U.S . merchants for every fraud dollar in 2025 is $4.61, meaning fraud losses multiply as they ripple through the system. For individual consumers, the cost is measured differently: hours disputing charges, waiting for replacement cards, updating payment details across every account that used the compromised card. Privacy cards reduce that blast radius to a single virtual number. Pro Tip: According to Privacy.com's support documentation , you can pause a virtual card between purchases to ensure fraudulent transactions can't slip through during a dormant period, a useful habit for cards tied to merchants you visit only occasionally. Privacy Cards for Subscription Management The Subscription Creep Problem Many people sign up for a free trial of a streaming service, a fitness app, or a productivity tool, and weeks or months later discover that money has been quietly draining from their account for a service they forgot they had. Subscription creep is real, and it adds unnecessary stress to already busy lives. The traditional solution involves digging through bank statements, tracking down login credentials, and navigating cancellation flows that are frequently designed to be frustrating. Privacy cards offer a cleaner alternative. How to Use Privacy Cards to Control Recurring Billing Instead of canceling subscriptions one by one, you can simply deactivate the virtual card tied to them, no emails, no begging support teams to stop charging you, just a quick tap in your app. This works because the merchant's billing system holds your virtual card number, and closing that number makes any future charge physically impossible to process. After setting a spending limit on your virtual card, the provider blocks all charges that exceed the preset limit. This feature helps you avoid intentional and accidental charges, such as double billing or price increases that you weren't aware of. If a streaming service quietly raises its monthly price, a tightly set spending limit will flag the attempt before it succeeds. The Envelope budgeting app takes this a step further by tying virtual debit cards directly to spending envelopes. Envelope lets you create virtual debit cards tied to specific envelopes, meaning the card is limited by the balance of the envelope it is connected to. For example, you could create a "Netflix" virtual debit card that only has $20 per month available, if the envelope doesn't have enough money, the card doesn't have extra money to pull from. Privacy Cards as a Budgeting Tool Spending Limits as Financial Guardrails Most people think of privacy cards purely as security tools, but their budgeting applications are equally powerful. Virtual cards provide granular control over spending, allowing users to set limits, expiration dates, and merchant restrictions, aiding in budgeting and preventing unauthorized use for both individuals and businesses. For individuals who struggle with consistent financial discipline, the ability to embed spending rules and limits directly into the payment mechanism makes managing a budget significantly easier and more sustainable. The limit enforces the budget at the moment of spending, rather than requiring you to review statements after the fact and recognize overspending that has already occurred. Category-Level Budget Control Category-locked cards can be used for multiple transactions with multiple merchants that belong to the same merchant category, such as groceries or dining. You can use these cards to budget and manage spending on specific products and services. Set a monthly cap on the category card, and the card itself prevents overspending, no willpower required. Pro Tip: Create one category-locked card for discretionary spending (dining, entertainment, personal care) and set its monthly limit to exactly what your budget allows. When the card declines, that's a real-time signal that the category is spent for the month, rather than a surprise you discover at month's end. What Privacy Cards Don't Protect Against Honest Limitations to Understand Privacy cards are a strong tool, but they have a defined scope. Virtual credit cards are not anonymous, unless they are cash-funded prepaid instruments. All other virtual cards remain tied to a verified identity due to Know Your Customer and Anti-Money Laundering rules. If complete financial anonymity is the goal, a privacy card from a standard provider won't achieve it. Some merchant categories block virtual cards entirely. Cryptocurrency exchanges are the most common example, but certain streaming platforms, cloud services, and gaming marketplaces occasionally require a traditional bank-issued card and will reject virtual card numbers. Always test with a small transaction before relying on a privacy card at a new merchant. Privacy cards do not affect your credit score in any direction. The provider does not run a credit check when you sign up, and your privacy card activity never appears on your credit report. This is a feature for those concerned about hard inquiries, but it also means privacy cards won't help you build credit history. What to Watch for on In-Person Purchases The most significant limitation of the privacy virtual card is that you cannot use it for in-store shopping. As there is no actual plastic card, only a number, it cannot be used anywhere except on the internet. Some providers now offer mobile wallet compatibility that extends virtual card use to in-person contactless terminals, but coverage varies by provider and region. Frequently Asked Questions What exactly is a privacy card and how is it different from a regular virtual card? A privacy card is usually a type of virtual card, and the terms often overlap, but the features matter more than the name. A basic virtual card may simply give you a separate card number, while a stronger privacy card may let you lock the card to one merchant, set spending limits, create one-time-use cards, pause or close cards instantly, and manage recurring bills. The distinguishing feature is control: a privacy card puts you in charge of how and where that number can be used. Are privacy cards safe to use? Privacy cards connect to your bank account, but merchants do not see your real account details. So even if a merchant is a scammer or its system gets hacked, your account details stay safe. The security comes from separation, the virtual number is the thing that gets exposed, not the real account it draws from. Providers like Privacy.com also use standard encryption protocols for data in transit and at rest. Can I use a privacy card for free trials? Yes, and this is one of their most practical applications. You can create a virtual card just for a trial subscription and set it to expire after one month. If you love the app, you can renew with a new card. If you don't, the old card expires and the company cannot bill you again. Set the spending limit to the exact cost of the trial period to be certain. Will a privacy card stop me from getting overcharged? Privacy cards let you set a spending limit to control how much a merchant can charge you. The card will decline all charges above that limit, helping protect you from hidden fees, duplicate charges, and other overcharges. The practical implication: set your spending limit to match the expected charge, and any attempt to bill more than that amount will be automatically declined. If the limit is hit unexpectedly, you receive a notification and can investigate before it becomes a dispute. Do privacy cards work everywhere online? Most major online merchants accept them, but there are exceptions. Some international merchants may also decline virtual card numbers. As noted earlier, certain categories, including cryptocurrency platforms and some gaming marketplaces, may require a card directly issued by a bank. Always have a backup payment method available. Testing with a small transaction before a large purchase is a reliable habit. The Bottom Line Privacy cards are a practical, low-cost way to reduce your exposure to card fraud, subscription overcharges, and the hassle of disputing unauthorized transactions. The fraud environment in 2025 and beyond makes waiting a genuinely costly choice: e-commerce fraud is projected to hit $107 billion by 2029, and every primary card number in a merchant's database is a potential target. Using a virtual card puts a disposable number between your real account and that risk. The smartest approach layers privacy cards with deliberate spending limits and a structured budgeting system. Tools like Envelope connect virtual debit cards to specific budget envelopes, so the spending guardrail is built in before the purchase ever happens. The result is a system where security and financial awareness reinforce each other rather than requiring separate effort. Start with one card, one merchant, one spending limit. title: The 9 Best Databases for AI Agents (August 2026): Features, Tradeoffs, and Use Cases
summary: This guide compares nine leading databases for AI agents, explains where each one excels, and helps you choose the right data infrastructure for your next AI application.
body_text: AI agents generate and consume far more data than traditional software applications. They store application state, retrieve knowledge, maintain conversation history, search embeddings, process documents, and analyze large datasets as they complete increasingly complex tasks. Traditional databases can support many of those workloads, but no single database is designed to handle all of them equally well. Different AI applications prioritize different kinds of data, retrieval methods, and performance requirements, leading developers to adopt a range of database architectures. Some platforms build on familiar relational databases with AI capabilities such as vector search. Others are purpose-built vector databases designed for semantic retrieval, while broader data platforms combine analytics, machine learning, and AI workloads within a unified environment. This guide focuses on nine of the leading database platforms developers are using to build AI agents. While the list is not exhaustive, it does cover many of the database technologies teams evaluate when building agentic systems. By the end of this roundup, you'll understand where each platform excels, the tradeoffs behind its design, and the types of AI applications it's best suited to support. What Is a Database for AI Agents? A database for AI agents stores and retrieves the information agents need to complete tasks. That information can take many forms. AI agents may store application state, user data, conversation history, documents, embeddings, search indexes, or the results of previous actions. As applications become more capable, they often rely on multiple kinds of data that need to be accessed quickly and reliably. Different databases are designed for different workloads. Relational databases organize structured application data, vector databases store embeddings for semantic search, document databases handle flexible data structures, and data platforms support large-scale analytics and machine learning. In addition, many production AI applications use more than one database. An agent might store user accounts and application state in PostgreSQL, retrieve knowledge from a vector database, cache frequently accessed data in Redis, and analyze historical data in a platform like Databricks. Choosing the right database depends on what your agent needs to store, how it retrieves information, and how the application is expected to scale. How to Evaluate a Database for AI Agents While every application has different requirements, we've found that these five considerations provide a useful starting point when evaluating databases for AI agents. Data Model Start by considering the type of data your agent needs to store. Relational databases organize structured application data, document databases support flexible schemas, vector databases store embeddings for semantic search, and data platforms manage large analytical datasets. Choosing a database that matches your primary workload can simplify development and improve long-term performance. Query and Retrieval Some applications primarily rely on SQL queries, while others depend on semantic search, metadata filtering, hybrid retrieval, or analytical queries across large datasets. Understanding how your agent accesses information will help narrow the field considerably. Scalability and Performance The database that works well during development may not be the right choice once your application reaches production. As AI applications grow, consider how each platform handles larger datasets, concurrent workloads, indexing, replication, latency, and operational scaling. The right architecture should continue performing reliably as both your users and data increase. AI-Native Capabilities Some databases have added AI capabilities over time, while others were built specifically for AI workloads. Features such as vector search, embedding storage, hybrid retrieval, and integrations with AI frameworks can reduce the amount of infrastructure developers need to build themselves. Which capabilities matter most depends on the type of application you're building. Developer Experience and Ecosystem Consider how easily each platform integrates with your existing programming languages, frameworks, deployment environment, and developer tools. Well-designed SDKs, documentation, and managed services can significantly reduce operational overhead as your application evolves. The 9 Best Databases for AI Agents 1. Databricks Lakebase Best for: Enterprise AI applications that need a transactional database tightly integrated with analytics, machine learning, and AI workloads. Databricks Lakebase is a fully managed PostgreSQL database integrated into the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. It combines low-latency transactional storage with native access to the broader Databricks ecosystem, allowing teams to build operational applications alongside analytics and AI workloads. Key capabilities include autoscaling, instant branching, and Unity Catalog integration. Lakebase is designed to support AI applications and agents. It can serve as a state store for AI agents, power application backends, and synchronize operational data with the lakehouse. It also supports semantic, keyword, and hybrid retrieval through Lakebase Search, allowing developers to combine transactional data with AI-powered search within the same PostgreSQL environment. For organizations already building on Databricks, Lakebase provides a transactional database that fits naturally into the broader data and AI platform. Teams can build operational applications while keeping application data closely connected to analytics, machine learning, and governed enterprise data. Why You Might Choose Databricks Lakebase Provides a fully managed PostgreSQL database for AI applications. Integrates transactional workloads with the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. Supports semantic, keyword, and hybrid retrieval through Lakebase Search. Keeps operational data closely connected to analytics and machine learning workloads. Scales automatically without requiring database infrastructure management. Includes built-in governance through Unity Catalog. Potential Tradeoffs Lakebase is designed for teams building on the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. Organizations looking for a standalone PostgreSQL service or a dedicated vector database may also want to evaluate more specialized alternatives. 2. Neon Best for: AI applications that need a serverless PostgreSQL database for transactional data, agent state, and modern development workflows. Neon is a serverless PostgreSQL platform that separates compute from storage, allowing each to scale independently. Developers get the full PostgreSQL experience while gaining capabilities such as instant branching, scale-to-zero compute, rapid provisioning, and fully managed infrastructure. For AI applications, Neon provides a foundation for storing structured application data, user information, workflow state, and agent state. It also supports vector storage and similarity search through the pgvector extension, allowing developers to combine transactional data and semantic retrieval within PostgreSQL for many AI workloads. In addition, Neon offers APIs, an MCP server, and the @neondatabase/toolkit to help AI agents create databases, run queries, and manage database operations programmatically. One of Neon's defining capabilities is database branching. Developers can create isolated copies of a database in seconds, making it easier to test new features, evaluate agent behavior, or experiment with different workflows without affecting production data. Combined with serverless scaling and PostgreSQL compatibility, this makes Neon a strong choice for teams building and iterating on AI-powered applications. Why You Might Choose Neon Provides a fully managed serverless PostgreSQL database. Separates compute and storage for independent autoscaling. Supports vector search through the pgvector extension. Creates instant database branches for development and testing. Includes APIs, an MCP server, and AI tooling for programmatic database management. Maintains full PostgreSQL compatibility with existing applications and tools. Potential Tradeoffs Neon is designed around PostgreSQL and operational application data. Teams building retrieval-heavy applications with very large embedding collections or highly specialized vector search requirements may also want to evaluate purpose-built vector databases alongside PostgreSQL. 3. MongoDB Best for: AI applications that need a flexible document database with integrated vector search and support for evolving data models. MongoDB is a document database that stores data in flexible BSON documents rather than fixed tables and rows. This document model makes it well suited for AI applications that work with user-generated content, conversation history, documents, and other data that may change structure over time. MongoDB Atlas, the company's fully managed cloud platform, includes Atlas Vector Search, allowing developers to combine operational data and vector search within the same database. Instead of maintaining separate systems for application data and semantic retrieval, developers can use MongoDB Atlas to support both workloads. Atlas Vector Search combines vector similarity search with metadata filtering, aggregation, and the broader MongoDB query language, making it easier to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and AI agents on a single platform. For teams already building on MongoDB, Atlas Vector Search extends an existing database with AI retrieval capabilities rather than requiring a separate vector database. This allows developers to introduce semantic search while continuing to use the same document model, APIs, and operational workflows. Why You Might Choose MongoDB Stores structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data in a flexible document model. Supports semantic retrieval through Atlas Vector Search. Combines vector search with metadata filtering and aggregation. Extends existing MongoDB applications with AI search capabilities. Integrates with popular AI frameworks and developer tools. Maintains operational and vector data within the same database. Potential Tradeoffs MongoDB is built around a document data model rather than PostgreSQL's relational model. Teams that rely heavily on SQL workflows or require advanced relational features may also want to evaluate PostgreSQL-based databases. 4. Redis Best for: AI applications that need low-latency data access, caching, and real-time application state. Redis is an in-memory data platform that stores data primarily in memory, enabling extremely low-latency reads and writes. Originally adopted for caching and session management, Redis has expanded to support vector search, semantic retrieval, and other AI workloads through Redis Query Engine. This makes it well suited for AI applications that need to retrieve and update data in milliseconds. For AI applications, Redis is commonly used to store session state, conversation history, cached retrieval results, and other latency-sensitive application data. Redis Query Engine also supports vector similarity search, allowing developers to combine semantic retrieval with operational data on the same platform for AI workloads where response time is critical. Redis is frequently used alongside other databases rather than replacing them. A production AI application might use PostgreSQL for transactional data, a vector database for long-term semantic retrieval, and Redis to accelerate frequently accessed data and reduce response times. This complementary architecture allows each database to handle the workload it is designed for. Why You Might Choose Redis Stores frequently accessed data in memory for low-latency access. Supports vector similarity search through Redis Query Engine. Accelerates AI applications with built-in caching capabilities. Manages session state and conversation history for AI applications. Integrates with popular AI frameworks and developer tools. Complements transactional and analytical databases in production architectures. Potential Tradeoffs Redis is designed for low-latency operational workloads rather than serving as a system of record for long-term application data. Teams building transactional applications or managing large analytical datasets will typically pair Redis with databases designed specifically for those workloads. 5. Pinecone Best for: AI applications that need a serverless vector database for production semantic search and retrieval. Pinecone is a serverless vector database built specifically for AI applications. It stores, indexes, and queries vector embeddings, allowing developers to retrieve information based on semantic similarity rather than exact keyword matches. This makes Pinecone well suited for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, recommendation systems, and AI agents that need to retrieve relevant context from large knowledge bases. Pinecone manages the infrastructure required to operate a production vector database, including indexing, scaling, replication, and filtering. It also supports metadata filtering, hybrid search, integrated inference models, and multitenant workloads, allowing developers to build production retrieval systems without managing the underlying infrastructure. Because Pinecone focuses exclusively on semantic retrieval, it is typically deployed alongside another database rather than replacing one. A common architecture pairs Pinecone with a relational or document database, using Pinecone to retrieve relevant context while the primary database continues to manage operational application data. Why You Might Choose Pinecone Provides a serverless vector database for AI applications. Optimizes semantic retrieval across large embedding collections. Supports metadata filtering alongside vector similarity search. Includes integrated inference models for retrieval workflows. Scales automatically without requiring infrastructure management. Integrates with popular AI frameworks and orchestration tools. Potential Tradeoffs Pinecone is designed specifically for semantic retrieval rather than transactional application data. Teams building AI applications typically pair it with a relational or document database that manages operational workloads. 6. Weaviate Best for: AI applications that need an open-source AI-native database with flexible retrieval and deployment options. Weaviate is an open-source AI-native vector database designed for semantic retrieval. It stores, indexes, and queries vector embeddings while also supporting keyword search, metadata filtering, and hybrid search. This allows developers to combine semantic and lexical retrieval within a single system, making Weaviate well suited for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), recommendation systems, and AI agents that search large collections of structured and unstructured data. One of Weaviate's defining characteristics is its modular architecture. Developers can choose from built-in vectorizers, integrate external embedding providers, and connect to leading LLMs for retrieval and generative AI workflows. Weaviate also supports reranking, multimodal search, and hybrid retrieval, giving teams flexibility to build AI applications around different models and retrieval strategies. Weaviate is available as both an open-source database and a fully managed cloud service. Organizations can self-host Weaviate, deploy it in their own cloud environment, or use Weaviate Cloud while maintaining the same core database architecture across environments. Why You Might Choose Weaviate Provides an open-source AI-native vector database. Supports semantic, keyword, and hybrid search. Integrates with leading embedding models and LLM providers. Enables multimodal retrieval across multiple data types. Offers both self-managed and fully managed deployment options. Supports metadata filtering alongside vector similarity search. Potential Tradeoffs Weaviate is designed specifically for AI retrieval rather than transactional application data. Teams building production AI applications typically pair it with a relational or document database that manages operational workloads. 7. Qdrant Best for: AI applications that need an open-source vector database with advanced filtering and production-scale semantic search. Qdrant is an open-source vector database built for semantic search and AI applications. It stores, indexes, and queries vector embeddings while combining vector similarity search with structured payload filtering. This allows developers to retrieve results based on both semantic meaning and structured metadata, making Qdrant well suited for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), recommendation systems, and AI agents that need precise, context-aware retrieval. One of Qdrant's key strengths is its filtering engine. Developers can combine vector similarity search with advanced payload filtering, payload indexing, and hybrid search to narrow retrieval results without sacrificing performance. Qdrant also supports multitenancy, distributed deployments, and quantization techniques for optimizing large-scale vector collections. Qdrant is available as both an open-source database and a fully managed cloud service. Organizations can self-host Qdrant for full infrastructure control or use Qdrant Cloud while maintaining the same APIs and core database architecture across environments. Why You Might Choose Qdrant Provides an open-source vector database for AI applications. Combines vector similarity search with advanced metadata filtering. Supports hybrid search across dense and sparse retrieval. Optimizes large vector collections with built-in quantization techniques. Offers both self-managed and fully managed deployment options. Integrates with popular AI frameworks and orchestration tools. Potential Tradeoffs Qdrant is designed specifically for semantic retrieval rather than transactional application data. Teams building production AI applications typically pair it with a relational or document database that manages operational workloads. 8. Milvus Best for: AI applications that need an open-source vector database for large-scale similarity search and distributed deployments. Milvus is an open-source vector database designed for storing, indexing, and querying high-dimensional vector embeddings. It supports multiple vector index types and similarity metrics, allowing developers to optimize retrieval for different AI workloads. This makes Milvus well suited for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), recommendation systems, image search, and AI agents that retrieve context from large embedding collections. Milvus uses a distributed architecture that allows organizations to scale the database across multiple nodes as datasets and query volumes grow. It also supports metadata filtering, hybrid search, multitenancy, and GPU acceleration for compatible workloads. Milvus is available as an open-source database and as a fully managed cloud service through Zilliz Cloud. Organizations can self-host Milvus for complete infrastructure control or use Zilliz Cloud while maintaining compatibility with the open-source project. Why You Might Choose Milvus Provides an open-source vector database for AI applications. Supports multiple indexing algorithms and similarity metrics. Scales distributed vector search across large datasets. Supports metadata filtering alongside vector similarity search. Offers both self-managed and fully managed deployment options. Integrates with popular AI frameworks and orchestration tools. Potential Tradeoffs Milvus is designed specifically for semantic retrieval rather than transactional application data. Teams building production AI applications typically pair it with a relational or document database that manages operational workloads. 9. PostgreSQL Best for: AI applications that need a relational database with a mature ecosystem and support for AI extensions. PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database that serves as the foundation for many modern applications. It stores structured data using tables, supports complex SQL queries, and offers a broad ecosystem of extensions that allow developers to add new capabilities without changing database platforms. For many AI applications, PostgreSQL acts as the system of record for users, application state, workflows, and transactional data. The PostgreSQL ecosystem has expanded to support AI workloads through extensions such as pgvector, which adds vector storage and similarity search. This allows developers to store embeddings alongside operational data and perform semantic retrieval within the same database. Depending on an application's scale and retrieval requirements, this can simplify the architecture by reducing the need for a separate vector database. Because PostgreSQL is widely supported across cloud providers, managed services, and development frameworks, it fits naturally into many existing software stacks. Teams can continue using familiar PostgreSQL tools and workflows while adding AI capabilities as retrieval, embeddings, and agent workflows become part of the application architecture. Why You Might Choose PostgreSQL Provides a mature relational database for AI applications. Supports vector search through the pgvector extension. Stores transactional data and embeddings within the same database. Integrates with a broad ecosystem of tools and managed services. Maintains compatibility with standard SQL and PostgreSQL applications. Extends existing PostgreSQL deployments with AI capabilities. Potential Tradeoffs PostgreSQL is designed as a general-purpose relational database rather than a purpose-built vector database. Applications with very large embedding collections or highly specialized semantic retrieval requirements may also want to evaluate dedicated vector databases. Which Database Should You Choose? Choose Databricks Lakebase if... You want a fully managed PostgreSQL database that keeps operational application data closely connected to analytics, machine learning, and governed enterprise data on the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. Choose Neon if... You want a serverless PostgreSQL database with autoscaling, database branching, and tooling that allows AI agents to manage database operations programmatically. Choose MongoDB if... You want to store flexible document data and add semantic retrieval through Atlas Vector Search without introducing a separate vector database. Choose Redis if... You need low-latency access to cached data, session state, conversation history, and other real-time application data. Choose Pinecone if... You want a serverless vector database that manages infrastructure for production semantic retrieval workloads. Choose Weaviate if... You want an open-source AI-native vector database with hybrid search, multimodal retrieval, flexible model integrations, and multiple deployment options. Choose Qdrant if... You want an open-source vector database that combines vector similarity search with advanced metadata filtering and hybrid retrieval. Choose Milvus if... You need distributed vector search across large embedding collections and want the flexibility to self-host the database or use Zilliz Cloud. Choose PostgreSQL if... You want a mature relational database and plan to add vector search through extensions such as pgvector while continuing to use familiar SQL workflows.

title: 8 Family-Friendly Spaces to Support Back-to-School Season at Home
summary: Discover 8 family-friendly spaces and organization ideas from Toll Brothers to help simplify routines and prepare your home for back-to-school season.
body_text: When the school year is back in full swing, family schedules quickly fill up, making organization and efficiency at home more important than ever. From managing homework and after-school activities to creating routines that keep everyone on track, the home is at the center of it all. Explore 8 family favorite spaces that shine during the back-to-school season and discover ways to make the most of the unique areas throughout your home. Whether it’s an at-home study space, a drop zone for backpacks, or a quiet place to focus, these spaces can help simplify daily routines and support a successful school year. Quick Summary A functional mudroom provides space for organization, including lockers, cubbies, and storage for backpacks, shoes, and everyday essentials. Simplify meal prep and daily routines with a walk-in pantry that serves as a hub for on-the-go breakfast options and after-school snacks. Kitchen islands are an oft-overlooked aspect of back-to-school season, providing ample space to pack lunch, complete homework, and stay connected throughout the day. Take a break from learning with innovative spaces like a home theater or a backyard putting green, ensuring a well-balanced mix of work and fun. Simplify school day routines with a functional mudroom Mudrooms are ideal spaces for keeping everyday essentials organized and reducing clutter throughout the home. Consider incorporating lockers, cubbies, or designated bins for each family member to store backpacks, shoes, sports gear, and other daily necessities, streamlining busy mornings and after-school routines. Parkside Village by Toll Brothers in Aldie, VA Stock up and stay organized with a walk-in pantry Walk-in pantries are a great place to keep school snacks and other supplies stored neatly and organized. Shelves or bins for grab-and-go breakfasts and after-school snacks can make busy mornings easier and help family routines run more smoothly during the school year. Woodson’s Reserve by Toll Brothers in Spring, TX Create a quiet place for work and study Home offices can provide a productive workspace for parents, as well as a quiet area for homework and studying for the kids. Having a dedicated space for focused work helps minimize distractions and supports productivity for the whole family. Toll Brothers at Maple Hills in Covington, WA Transform flexible spaces into study areas Flex rooms can easily adapt to a variety of back-to-school needs, from homework stations and reading nooks to creative craft areas and study spaces. These versatile rooms allow families to customize the space to fit their unique routines, creating a dedicated environment that supports learning, creativity, and productivity for kids of all ages. Tribute at Valor by Toll Brothers in Kuna, ID Gather, prep, and connect around the kitchen island Kitchens are always a natural gathering space, especially for meals, homework, and family conversations. Islands provide extra seating for quick meals and added space for packing lunches or catching up at the end of the day. Toll Brothers at Elk Ridge in Elk Ridge, UT Use a loft as an extra space for learning and leisure Lofts are a versatile space for studying, reading, and unwinding after a busy school day. Their flexible design allows them to accommodate a variety of activities while adapting to changing household needs over time. As children grow and routines evolve, lofts can easily transform and support every stage of family life. Saddlecrest at Windermere by Toll Brothers in Windermere, FL Enjoy family time in a home theater Create an entertainment destination without ever leaving home with a dedicated home theater. This inviting space is perfect for family movie nights, weekend downtime, and gathering to enjoy your favorite shows, sporting events, or games. With comfortable seating and an immersive viewing experience, a home theater offers a fun way for families to relax, reconnect, and make lasting memories throughout the school year. Shavano Highlands by Toll Brothers in San Antonio, TX Extend learning and play outdoors Outdoor spaces can extend living and entertaining beyond the home’s interior. They are perfect for reading and studying in nice weather, as well as for family gatherings and weekend activities. With room to play, exercise, and enjoy fresh air, these areas offer a balance of relaxation and recreation. Toll Brothers at The Crossing at Coal Mountain in Cumming, GA For more organization and design inspiration for your home, visit the Dream Design category on our Build Beautiful blog.

title: SEALSQ Highlights Growing Importance of Hardware-Based Crypto-Agility as AI Accelerates Cryptanalysis
summary: AI-assisted cryptanalysis highlights the need for crypto-agile hardware. Discover how SEALSQ embeds post-quantum security and trust into silicon.
body_text: Recent AI-assisted cryptanalysis research reinforces the need for standardized post-quantum cryptography, hardware Roots of Trust and the ability to securely evolve cryptographic algorithms throughout a device’s lifecycle Geneva, Switzerland – August 3, 2026 – SEALSQ Corp (NASDAQ: LAES) (“SEALSQ” or the “Company”), a global leader in post-quantum semiconductor and cybersecurity technology, today highlighted the growing importance of crypto-agile hardware architectures in light of new research into how artificial intelligence can accelerate the discovery of potential weaknesses in cryptographic algorithms , and compress the timeframe in which organizations must respond to emerging threats. Recent research discussed by PostQuantum.com examines AI-assisted cryptanalysis involving HAWK, a post-quantum signature candidate, as well as advances in attacks against reduced-round AES-128. Importantly, these findings do not demonstrate the breaking of NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM or ML-DSA, nor do they represent a practical break of full 10-round AES-128. Nevertheless, SEALSQ believes the broader implication is significant: AI could substantially accelerate the cryptographic research and attack cycle, potentially reduce the time required to identify structural weaknesses in algorithms and implementations. This evolution reinforces SEALSQ’s strategy of embedding post-quantum security, hardware Roots of Trust and crypto-agility directly into semiconductor architectures, enabling customers to treat security as an upgradable capability at the chip level rather than a fixed design choice made at deployment. “AI is not breaking post-quantum cryptography today, but it is changing the speed at which cryptographic systems can be analyzed,” said Carlos Moreira, CEO of SEALSQ. “The security industry must therefore move beyond the assumption that a cryptographic algorithm deployed today will remain unchanged for the next 20 years. The future requires crypto-agile hardware capable of securely adapting as algorithms, standards and threats evolve, a capability that we believe will become a differentiating factor for manufacturers seeking to protect long-duration revenue streams and enhance the resilience of their installed base” From Static Cryptography to Crypto-Agile Silicon SEALSQ’s post-quantum semiconductor strategy is designed around the principle that long-lived connected devices require more than a single cryptographic algorithm. Through technologies including its QS7001 post-quantum secure microcontroller platform, SEALSQ is developing hardware capable of combining classical and post-quantum cryptography while providing secure key storage, trusted device identity, secure boot, cryptographic acceleration and authenticated firmware updates. The QS7001 architecture is designed around NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms, including ML-KEM and ML-DSA, providing a hardware foundation for manufacturers preparing products and infrastructure for the post-quantum era. Crypto-agility is particularly important for devices expected to remain operational for 10, 20 or more years, including industrial systems, automotive platforms, smart grids, telecommunications infrastructure, satellites, defense systems, medical equipment and billions of IoT devices. If an algorithm or parameter set needs to be replaced during the lifetime of such infrastructure, the ability to securely authenticate and deploy cryptographic updates becomes critical. AI and Quantum Computing Are Converging Into a New Security Challenge SEALSQ believes cybersecurity is entering an era in which two disruptive technologies must be considered simultaneously : quantum computing as a structural challenge to widely deployed public-key cryptography, and AI as an accelerator of vulnerability discovery, exploitation and automation. Quantum computing creates the long-term threat of breaking widely deployed public-key cryptography, while artificial intelligence could increasingly accelerate vulnerability discovery, cryptanalysis and automated cyberattacks. Together, these developments increase the urgency of migrating critical digital infrastructure toward post-quantum and crypto-agile security architectures. The Company believes the response must begin at the semiconductor level. By establishing a trusted hardware foundation for cryptographic operations, device identities, key protection and secure updates, hardware Roots of Trust can provide the infrastructure necessary to adapt cryptographic protections as the threat environment changes. Building the Trust Infrastructure for the Post-Quantum Era SEALSQ’s strategy extends beyond individual cryptographic algorithms toward a broader sovereign security architecture in which trusted semiconductor hardware forms the foundation for post-quantum digital identities, secure communications and future quantum infrastructure. Mr. Moreira added: “The lesson from AI-assisted cryptanalysis is not that post-quantum cryptography has failed. It is that cryptography itself is becoming increasingly dynamic. Algorithms will evolve, attacks will evolve and standards will evolve. Our objective at SEALSQ is to anchor that dynamism in trusted silicon, giving customers hardware that can adapt with changing algorithms and requirements as regulatory expectations tighten and stakeholders focus more intensely on cyber resilience.” SEALSQ believes this transition from static encryption to continuously adaptable trust infrastructure will become increasingly important as governments, enterprises and critical infrastructure operators prepare for the convergence of AI, quantum computing and next-generation cybersecurity threats. About SEALSQ: SEALSQ is a leading innovator in Post-Quantum Technology hardware and software solutions. Our technology seamlessly integrates Semiconductors, PKI (Public Key Infrastructure), and Provisioning Services, with a strategic emphasis on developing state-of-the-art Quantum Resistant Cryptography and Semiconductors designed to address the urgent security challenges posed by quantum computing. As quantum computers advance, traditional cryptographic methods like RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) are increasingly vulnerable. SEALSQ is pioneering the development of Post-Quantum Semiconductors that provide robust, future-proof protection for sensitive data across a wide range of applications, including Multi-Factor Authentication tokens, Smart Energy, Medical and Healthcare Systems, Defense, IT Network Infrastructure, Automotive, and Industrial Automation and Control Systems. By embedding Post-Quantum Cryptography into our semiconductor solutions, SEALSQ ensures that organizations stay protected against quantum threats. Our products are engineered to safeguard critical systems, enhancing resilience and security across diverse industries. For more information on our Post-Quantum Semiconductors and security solutions, please visit www.sealsq.com . title: The Pioneering History of Briggs Cunningham’s Stanguellini Formula Junior
summary: If your summer plans include a visit to Laguna Seca to catch the Monterey Motorsports Reunion, or Lime Rock for the Historic Festival, or Watkins Glen for the Vintage Grand Prix weekend, be on the lookout for the little blue Stanguellini. This unassuming front-engine open-wheeler has a history that belies its on-track stature, and it […]
body_text: If your summer plans include a visit to Laguna Seca to catch the Monterey Motorsports Reunion, or Lime Rock for the Historic Festival, or Watkins Glen for the Vintage Grand Prix weekend, be on the lookout for the little blue Stanguellini. This unassuming front-engine open-wheeler has a history that belies its on-track stature, and it began nearly 70 years ago with American sportsman Briggs Cunningham . Cunningham is maybe best known for the eponymously named race cars he valiantly campaigned in the 24 Hours of Le Mans from 1950 to 1955. Although his prodigious racing resume boasts two class wins at the French classic, along with three more at Sebring, one might argue that Cunningham’s most significant contribution to American motorsports was his introduction and promotion of an affordable, entry-level racing category that would lay the groundwork for all the American open-wheeled ladder series to follow. From Privateer to Constructor and Back Cunningham’s early years of racing began as a privateer, in the 1930s, campaigning an MG J2 alongside his college friends the Collier brothers. But it didn’t take long before he began to seek out ever faster and more competitive machinery with which to enter the granddaddy of all sports car races, the 24 Hours of Le Mans . Cunningham’s obsession with winning Le Mans would see him eventually turn to constructing his own cars, which made their Le Mans debut in 1950. Briggs Cunningham in a C4R at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, 1954. Getty Images After five years of building and racing his own machinery, however, with a fourth place overall and first in class in a C-2R in 1952 as his best showing, Cunningham wrapped up his carmaking business—not due to lack of interest or success, but because the Internal Revenue Service only allowed a business to run at a loss for five consecutive years before declaring it no longer a viable concern. Although Cunningham was the consummate sportsman, he was also savvy enough to understand when the Cunningham Car Company had run its useful course. By the late 1950s, Cunningham had returned to his early ways as a privateer, and he campaigned a host of competitive machinery in various American sports car categories. He fielded a series of Jaguar D-Types and Lister Jaguars during this period, but he had also begun dabbling with Italian machinery. Cunningham had run the first Ferrari in the United States, in 1949, and he followed that up with a steady trickle of Maseratis, OSCAs, and even a diminutive 750-cc Stanguellini H-Mod, which won its class at Watkins Glen in 1954, in the hands of Marshall Lewis. Little did anyone know then that this car would lead to much bigger things. Since Cunningham and his lead driver, Walt Hansgen, had been successfully campaigning Lister Jaguars in the U.S., Hansgen was invited to drive one of the factory Lister Sport entries at Le Mans in 1959. Cunningham and mechanic Alfred Momo tagged along in support. Hansgen’s car expired after five hours with engine trouble, so Cunningham and Momo made a side trip down to Modena to check on the latest offerings from Ferrari, Maserati, and the oldest manufacturer in the city, the workshops of Vittorio Stanguellini. Automobili Stanguellini Stanguellini.it As early as 1900, Francesco Stanguellini began constructing his own racing trikes and automobiles within the walls of the timpani drum manufacturing business he had inherited from his father. It wasn’t long before drums were ditched and Stanguellini became the first Fiat agent in Modena. Francesco passed away in 1932, leaving the business to his son Vittorio. The younger Stanguellini shared his father’s passion for racing and, like Carlo Abarth and numerous other Italian automotive entrepreneurs of the postwar period, he built a reputation for himself by “hoppin’ up” Fiat engines and componentry for racing. Vittorio started with Fiat sedans in 1935, but by 1946 he had constructed his own, purpose-built sports car using Fiat components. Three years later, Stanguellini produced its first single-seater race car, powered by a 1.1-liter engine. The car was tested by no less than Alberto Ascari before being raced to its first win in the 1100-cc category of the 1950 Circuito del Garda in the hands of Sergio Sighinolfi. In fact, not only did Sighinolfi handily win his class, he also finished an impressive fifth overall in the larger-displacement F2 category, which was won by Ascari in a Ferrari 166. The 1950s would see Stanguellini go on to create a host of elegant and competitive small-displacement sports racers using modified variations of Fiat’s venerable 750-cc inline-four engine. One of those jewel-like machines even found success on the other side of the globe in the racing stable of Briggs Cunningham. Then, in 1957, another wealthy sportsman, Count Giovanni “Johnny” Lurani, approached Stanguellini with a proposition. Lurani was stumping to create an affordable, entry-level category for Italian drivers to get started in open-wheel racing. His idea was to create a series of simple, ladder-frame race cars that could only use small-displacement production engines and componentry derived from inexpensive homologated touring cars. Since Stanguellini had already produced a successful 1100-cc formula car back in 1950, Vittorio enthusiastically embraced Lurani’s new initiative. Birth of the Junior Stanguellini.it The creation of Stanguellini’s prototype “Formula Junior,” as it would come to be known, was entrusted to engineer Alberto Massimino. Massimino had quite a pedigree, having worked under Vittorio Jano at Fiat and Alfa Romeo before moving on to stints with Ferrari and Maserati. By the late 1950s, Massimino was working as a freelance consultant specializing in chassis and suspension design. For Stanguellini, he had already consulted on the 1100 Sport before being given the commission to work on the new Formula Junior. He laid out a relatively simple, easy-to-repair, ladder-frame chassis constructed of two 80-mm longitudinal steel side members, joined by six smaller-diameter crossmembers with a stressed skin floorpan for added rigidity. A small-tube substructure was then welded on to provide additional bracing and the ability to hang the car’s 16-gallon fuel tank and aluminum bodywork. For the suspension, Massimino used the independent front wishbone arrangement derived from the Fiat 1100/103, while at the rear he incorporated the same Fiat’s live rear axle with parallel trailing arms for location. Stanguellini Power was, of course, provided by Fiat’s 1100-cc, OHV inline-four. Capable of producing 78 horsepower at 6500 rpm, Stanguellini’s tuned little buzzbomb of an engine transmitted its power through a standard Fiat 1100 four-speed gearbox that had been modified to accept close-ratio gears and a central shifter. Although Massimino was limited in what he could do with this powertrain, he was clever in the way that he installed it in his chassis. By placing the engine and gearbox slightly askew in the chassis—at a 9-degree angle relative to the longitudinal axis—Massimino was able to run the driveline alongside the driver in the cockpit, thus freeing him to seat the driver much lower in the car. This lowered the car’s center of gravity and gave it improved handling. The Stanguellini was then clothed in a beautiful aluminum body penned by Franco Reggiani and hammer-formed by the craftsmen at Carrozzeria Gransport. If the result looked like a scaled-down version of the famed Maserati 250F, that was no accident, as Massimino had been one of the key architects of that car as well. As such, it may not be surprising that when it came time to shake down the new Formula Junior, Massimino turned to a trusted friend from his days with Maserati—Juan Manuel Fangio. Fangio tested the Stanguellini prototype at the Modena Autodrome in 1957 and provided invaluable feedback. With the new car now Fangio-approved and fully sorted, it was ready to contend the first Italian National Formula Junior championship. A New Class of Racing Stanguellini.it The inaugural race of Lurani’s new Italian Formula Junior Championship took place at Monza on April 25, 1958, and was won by Roberto Lippi driving the Stanguellini. In fact, Lippi would go on to post wins at two subsequent Vallelunga events, a win at Modena and a second-place finish at the second Monza event to claim the first Formula Junior championship for himself and Stanguellini. The following year would reaffirm Stanguellini’s dominance with another Italian National Championship, this time in the hands of Raffaele Cammarota. Driver Michael May claimed the first International Formula Junior Championship as well, with wins at Monaco, Solitude, and the Nürburgring. That 1959 International season was also notable for Stanguellini wins in the hands of two promising up-and-coming drivers: Lorenzo Bandini (at Innsbruck) and Wolfgang von Trips (at the Eifelrennen). With such dominant performances in such a short period of time, it is no wonder that in the summer of 1959, Cunningham and Momo paid their visit to Modena to see what all the buzz was about. Stanguellini Formula Junior in Oporto, 1958. Getty Images Maria Teresa de Filippis, the first woman to compete in Formula 1, also raced in a Stanguellini FJ, seen here at Monaco in 1959. National Motor Museum/Heritage I Rob Slotemaker in a Ford Lola leads the #26 Stanguellini of Gastone Zanarotti at Monza, 1961. The emergence of mid-engine machinery had already taken hold in Formula Junior and elsewhere. Getty Images Briggs Cunningham was impressed enough with the new Stanguellini that he not only ordered one to be air-shipped to the States as soon as possible, but he also arranged to become the official U.S. importer, via Alfred Momo’s Momo Corporation. That first U.S. car, chassis 00139, was built July 10, 1959, and made its debut a month later at the SCCA National event at Montgomery, New York, in the hands of team driver Walt Hansgen. Since 00139 was the only Formula Junior in the country at that time, it was allowed to run as an exhibition in the G- and H-Modified race, where Hansgen still managed to finish in second overall. From there, Hansgen and 00139 went to Connecticut’s Thompson Raceway, where he finished third overall and second in the unrestricted class. At Road America on September 12, Hansgen claimed an overall victory in the Stanguellini, though he was awarded no points, because again there were no other Formula Juniors to make up a class. Finally, on September 26, at Watkins Glen, Hansgen drove the Stanguellini to overall victory in the Seneca Cup. There he not only beat his sports car nemesis, George Constantine, in an Aston Martin DBR2, but he beat an Elva Formula Junior and two Cooper F3 cars to also win the newly created Formula Junior category, thus marking 00139 as the first officially sanctioned “FJr.” winner in the United States. Briggs Cunningham in 00139, with Count “Johnny” Lurani at left. Courtesy Peter Fenichel Walt Hansgen in 00139 at Watkins Glen, 1959 Courtesy Peter Fenichel With such momentum, Momo and Cunningham then embarked on a major effort to promote Formula Junior in the U.S., offering $5000 in sponsorship to the organizers of the 1959 Sebring U.S. Grand Prix that December to stage the first all-Formula Junior race, in support of the Grand Prix. To ensure a good entry for the Sebring race, Cunningham organized two test days in September at Bridgehampton Race Circuit, where prospective customers could test-drive chassis 00139. The session resulted in nine orders, which, one could argue, made 00139 instrumental in the promotion of Formula Junior in the U.S. This in turn laid the groundwork for every entry-level American open-wheeled series that followed. Even with this lofty legacy, chassis 00139 had one more record to break. The field for the Formula Junior support race at the 1959 U.S. Grand Prix was dominated by Stanguellinis. Hansgen, in car #1, is in the middle of the first row of the grid. The Henry Ford At that December’s U.S. Grand Prix, Cunningham entered two Stanguellinis in the Formula Junior support race—chassis 00139 for Hansgen, and chassis 00179 for himself. Of the 22 cars entered for this inaugural Formula Junior field, 12 were Stanguellinis. With such a loaded field, it should come as no surprise that the top seven finishers were the mini-250Fs from Modena, with Hansgen handily taking the victory over the Stanguellinis of Fritz d’Orey, Ed Hugus, and Cunningham, in fourth place. Stanguellini produced more than 100 of its front-engine single-seaters before 1963, though their initial successes were soon rivaled with the introduction of mid-engine entries from the likes of Cooper and Lotus. After… 00139 sold to England in 1980, and a subsequent restoration resulted in red paintwork. It is seen here with previous owner Gordon Wright at Oulton Park. Courtesy Peter Fenichel Following its Sebring success, Cunningham sold chassis 00139. The car moved through a succession of owners in the New York area, and at some point it is believed the Stanguellini was refitted with an Alfa Romeo engine and raced as a Formula Libre car. By 1980, in a sad state, it sold to the U.K. before being restored over a three-year period by a fellow named Brian Horwood and finished in red. He campaigned 00139 for three years before selling it, and from 1986 to 2003, collector and amateur racer Martin Bunn piloted the car extensively at historic events in the U.K. and Europe. Under his care, the Stanguellini was invited to participate in the inaugural Goodwood Revival in 1998, and again in 2003. Fellow Brit Gordon Wright, who campaigned the Stanguellini successfully from 2005 to 2015, claimed the Front-Engine title for the Formula Junior Historic Racing Association in 2007, among other crowns. A shunt at Silverstone in 2007 required a rebuild, however. Traces of the car’s original blue paint were discovered during that process, so the shell was stripped and repainted in its original livery. 00139, blue once again, in action at the Zandvoort Historic Grand Prix, 2024. Maurice Volmeyer The car’s current owner, Peter Fenichel, purchased it in 2015, raced it in Europe for a couple of seasons, including at the 2016 Grand Prix de Monaco Historique, then sold it in 2017, only to buy it once more in 2022, this time from Gooding Christie’s London Auction. In his hands it has since been crowned the 2023 and 2024 Formula Junior Class A Champion. Fenichel began racing cars in the U.K. and Europe in the 1990s through the Vintage Sports Car Club, primarily piloting a Lagonda Rapier and MG K-Type Special. He first tried his hand in Formula Junior with a Cooper T56 in 2010 because, as he puts it, “something safer was the objective.” He spent more than 10 years with the Cooper and only sold it after reacquiring the Stanguellini. Courtesy Peter Fenichel Courtesy Peter Fenichel Courtesy Peter Fenichel Courtesy Peter Fenichel Courtesy Peter Fenichel Fenichel behind the wheel of the Stanguellini at the 2016 Grand Prix de Monaco Historique. “Driving rear-engine FJs, or for that matter any rear-engine race car, is quite different from the earlier tech of front-engine race cars,” he says. “My experience with FJs is that the later rear-engine cars pretty much go where you point them, are clearly quicker than earlier engine tech, and with developments in chassis design corner with greater speed and handling. The Stanguellini habitually understeers, and the obvious weight in the front makes cornering rather an acquired art. But, while I find the Stanguellini more of a challenge to drive, I prefer that to what a ‘boy racer’ might.” For Fenichel, there is also the undeniable appeal of this particular Stanguellini. “I just get a kick out of doing the best I can driving, with that historic equipment.” Fenichel’s summer plans include a grand homecoming for the Stanguellini. He and the car will be in the U.S. to run a series of premium Formula Junior events that includes the Monterey Rolex Reunion (and Pre-Reunion) and then the Lime Rock Historic Festival in September. But the story will come full circle later in the month when Fenichel brings the Stanguellini back to where it all began 67 years ago—Watkins Glen—for the Vintage Grand Prix. There he’ll be sharing the track with the ghosts of Briggs Cunningham and Walt Hansgen, piloting the car that changed the face of American open-wheel racing forever.
